newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran court acquits editor of slandering minister.
newsitem.headline: Iran court acquits editor of slandering minister.

text.p: An Iranian court has found the editor of a hardline Islamic weekly not guilty of slander for articles accusing Iran's telecommunications minister of financial mismanagement, Tehran newspapers said on Tuesday.
The daily Salam said the court acquitted Mehdi Nassiri, editor of the Islamic weekly Sobh, of charges of slander and confusing public opinion.
The court found Nassiri guilty of insulting Post and Telecommunication Minister Mohammad Gharazi but did not punish the editor, ruling that he had "good intentions".

Sobh had accused Gharazi of favouritism in delivering telephone services to officials, breach of budgetary guidelines, questionable practices in granting foreign contracts and wasting ministry funds on chartered planes and helicopters.

Some parliament deputies last year criticised a deal between Iran's state telecommunications company and Finland's Nokia for 260,000 mobile phones, saying a local company could have delivered cheaper telephones of equal quality.
The daily Kayhan, which is politically close to Sobh, suggested authorities should investigate the ministry's affairs following the verdict. No official probe has been launched.
Sobh has been allied with conservative critics of outgoing President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani and has blasted government bodies for alleged corruption and mismanagement.
The court ruling came as newspapers and parliament deputies continued demands for tough action against alleged corruption among state officials.

Iranian analysts said the demands appeared orchestrated by the conservatives against moderate officials close to Rafsanjani and president-elect Mohammad Khatami who is due to take over on August 3. Khatami defeated the conservatives' candidate, parliament speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, by a landslide in May.
A majority of parliamentary deputies earlier this month called for an investigation into the assets of top officials of Rafsanjani's administration and their families.
Iranian supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei had earlier called on the judiciary to confront the misuse of public funds, which he described as a "dangerous phenomenon".
An Iranian court last month sentenced a state official and 12 accomplices to up to 30 years in jail for misappropriating large sums of state funds earmarked for earthquake-hit areas.
A former Revolutionary Guards commander is on trial on treason and embezzlement charges.
The cases followed a series of trials for embezzlement and fraud at state agencies and banks in the past few years that have featured prominently in the local media and sparked wide public outcry.
